The Food Safety Department seized 508 kg of spurious paneer at Okhla Sabzi Mandi earlier this month. | Photo Credit: liubomirt
As sacks of khoya and paneer arrive in Delhi’s markets and sweet shops stock up for the festive rush, the Delhi Police Crime Branch is stepping up intelligence-gathering on food adulteration.

The watch comes amid a series of food safety seizures and inspections across Delhi. More than 2,800 kg of unsafe and abandoned khoya and butter were found in major markets earlier this month. Ten khoya and cream samples collected from Mori Gate were found to be non-conforming, while four paneer samples from Janakpuri Mandi tested positive for detergent. Around 150 kg of paneer and 10 kg of khoya were subsequently destroyed.

The Food Safety Department also seized 508 kg of spurious paneer at Okhla Sabzi Mandi and destroyed over 131 kg of expired food items, including gram flour, khoya and wheat flour, during inspections of sweet manufacturing units and mandis.

“With the festive season approaching, the Crime Branch has been on alert to identify leads related to food adulteration. As soon as we receive information about food adulteration, it is shared with the Delhi government’s Food Safety Department. The information and timing of the operation are coordinated with the department, following which joint raids are conducted,” said Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) H.G.S. Dhaliwal.

The police, however, do not independently test suspected food products. Deputy Commissioner of Police (Crime) Aditya Gautam said food safety officers accompanying the police during raids collect samples for laboratory testing.

Mr. Gautam said investigators had found rangkat or hydro powder (sodium hydrosulfite), being used to give khoya and sweets a whiter appearance, sawdust mixed with cumin, brick powder with chilli powder, and chemicals and hydrogenated vegetable oil used to adulterate ghee.
Speaking to The Hindu, Devesh Mahla, Director, Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) - North India, said the nature of milk adulteration has also changed.

“Earlier, they used to mix water in milk, which was not necessarily dangerous, but now, as the demand and greed have increased, they have started preparing synthetic milk made of chemicals, including detergents, shampoo, caustic soda and urea,” he said.
Mr. Gautam said accused persons often change locations after an operation, making subsequent raids at the same premises uncommon.
Mr. Mahla said, raids were based on consumer complaints and risk-based assessment of food items. Milk, meat, ghee, khoya and eggs are among the categories assessed as higher risk, he said.

Food safety officers are authorised under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, to inspect premises, verify FSSAI licences and documents and collect samples for laboratory testing. “The report is used to prosecute the offender,” Mr. Mahla said.

Mr. Mahla said registered food businesses could be subjected to regular surveillance, surprise inspections and sampling, while unregistered establishments, including roadside food vendors and outlets in food streets, often remained outside routine surveillance until a complaint is received.

Depending on the nature of the offence, police can invoke Sections 274 and 275 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for food adulteration and the sale of noxious or unfit food, and Section 318 in cases of cheating. Provisions relating to tampering with or counterfeiting property marks can be invoked when fake packaging or brands are used. Sections 105 and 110, dealing with culpable homicide not amounting to murder and attempt to commit culpable homicide, respectively, may apply if adulteration causes death or serious injury.

Mr. Mahla urged consumers to check whether food businesses have the appropriate FSSAI registration or licence and to be aware of what they are consuming. Suspected adulteration can be reported through FSSAI’s Food Safety Connect platform or its official website.
